claim: The anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) is thought to play an important role in a brain network involving the hippocampus and neocortex, which enables human memories to be formed.
source: The anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) is thought to play an important role in a brain network involving the hippocampus and neocortex, which enables human memories to be formed.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established theoretical understanding in the field.

claim: The small size and deep location of the ATN within the brain have impeded direct investigation in humans with non-invasive techniques.
source: However, its small size and location deep within the brain have impeded direct investigation in humans with non-invasive techniques.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical challenges of studying the ATN, based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Simultaneous intrathalamic and scalp EEG recordings were obtained from eight volunteering patients receiving intrathalamic electrodes implanted for the treatment of epilepsy.
source: Here we provide direct evidence for a functional role for the ATN in memory formation from rare simultaneous human intrathalamic and scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings from eight volunteering patients receiving intrathalamic electrodes implanted for the treatment of epilepsy
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and data collection from patients.

claim: Neocortical-ATN theta oscillatory phase synchrony of local field potentials during presentation of complex photographic scenes predicted later memory for the scenes.
source: Neocortical-ATN theta oscillatory phase synchrony of local field potentials and neocortical-theta-to-ATN-gamma cross-frequency coupling during presentation of complex photographic scenes predicted later memory for the scenes
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neocortical-theta-to-ATN-gamma cross-frequency coupling during presentation of complex photographic scenes predicted later memory for the scenes.
source: Neocortical-ATN theta oscillatory phase synchrony of local field potentials and neocortical-theta-to-ATN-gamma cross-frequency coupling during presentation of complex photographic scenes predicted later memory for the scenes
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The findings demonstrate a key role for the ATN in human memory encoding.
source: demonstrating a key role for the ATN in human memory encoding.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The anterior thalamic nuclei (ATN) are thought to play an important role in an extended hippocampal network central to memory formation (encoding) and novelty processing.
source: The anterior thalamic nuclei (ATN) are thought to play an important role in an extended hippocampal network central to memory formation (encoding) and novelty processing, which coordinates synaptic changes involving widespread neocortical areas, enabling life events to be recorded and later reinstated (Knight, 1996; Aggleton et al., 2010; Nyhus and Curran, 2011; Ritchey et al., 2013; Schott et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The extended hippocampal network coordinates synaptic changes involving widespread neocortical areas, enabling life events to be recorded and later reinstated.
source: The anterior thalamic nuclei (ATN) are thought to play an important role in an extended hippocampal network central to memory formation (encoding) and novelty processing, which coordinates synaptic changes involving widespread neocortical areas, enabling life events to be recorded and later reinstated (Knight, 1996; Aggleton et al., 2010; Nyhus and Curran, 2011; Ritchey et al., 2013; Schott et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Corticothalamic interactions are crucial for adaptive behavior.
source: While corticothalamic interactions are well-known to be crucial for adaptive behavior (Saalmann et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The functional role of the ATN in humans has resisted investigation with non-invasive techniques owing both to its depth and small size.
source: the functional role of the ATN in humans has resisted investigation with non-invasive techniques owing both to its depth and small size.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical challenges of studying the ATN, based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Electrophysiological activity was recorded during memory encoding directly from the ATN and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei (DMTN) of eight epileptic human volunteers with electrodes implanted for epilepsy treatment.
source: Here we had the rare opportunity to record electrophysiological activity during memory encoding directly from the ATN and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei (DMTN) of eight epileptic human volunteers with electrodes implanted for epilepsy treatment
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and data collection.

claim: Electrophysiological activity was recorded from frontal (and in two cases, parietal) scalp electrodes, reflecting neocortical activity.
source: as well as from frontal (and in two cases, parietal) scalp electrodes, reflecting neocortical activity (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and data collection, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The DMTN are thought to be involved in executive control during memory retrieval.
source: The DMTN are thought to be involved in executive control during memory retrieval (Van der Werf et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The DMTN were hypothesized to play a lesser role than the ATN during encoding.
source: and were hypothesized to play a lesser role than the ATN during encoding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on prior knowledge.

claim: Damage to the human ATN results in amnesia for new episodes.
source: Damage to the human ATN results in amnesia for new episodes (Harding et al., 2000; Van der Werf et al., 2003; Aggleton et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on human lesion studies.

claim: Reciprocal frontal and parietal connections with the ATN have led to the hypothesis that ATN-hippocampal connections play a regulatory role in encoding.
source: and reciprocal frontal and parietal connections with the ATN (Aggleton, 2012) have led to the hypothesis that ATN-hippocampal connections play a regulatory role in encoding (Vertes et al., 2001; Aggleton et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 75% of ATN oscillatory power in non-human animal studies is in the theta (4–8 Hz) range.
source: Notably, 75% of ATN oscillatory power in non-human animal studies is in the theta (4–8 Hz) range, the dominant hippocampal rhythm (Vertes et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior animal research.

claim: Theta (4–8 Hz) is the dominant hippocampal rhythm.
source: Notably, 75% of ATN oscillatory power in non-human animal studies is in the theta (4–8 Hz) range, the dominant hippocampal rhythm (Vertes et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Theta oscillations are implicated in ATN-hippocampal communication.
source: which is also implicated in ATN-hippocampal communication (Vertes et al., 2001; Aggleton et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural communication and synaptic plasticity rely on long-range phase–phase and phase–amplitude synchrony of neural oscillations.
source: Neural communication and synaptic plasticity rely on long-range phase–phase and phase–amplitude synchrony of neural oscillations (Lachaux et al., 1999; Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Fronto-hippocampal theta synchrony accompanies memory formation.
source: Fronto-hippocampal theta synchrony accompanies memory formation (Benchenane et al., 2010; Nyhus and Curran, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Theta synchrony is reported to bind medial temporal (MT) and parietal areas during associative encoding.
source: Furthermore, theta synchrony is reported to bind medial temporal (MT) and parietal areas during associative encoding (Crespo-Garcia et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Theta synchrony binds MT with frontal and parietal cortex during successful retrieval.
source: and MT with frontal and parietal cortex during successful retrieval (Watrous et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Neocortical and hippocampal gamma (>30 Hz) oscillations appear to reflect local processing related to activation and maintenance of neuronal object representations.
source: Neocortical and hippocampal gamma (>30 Hz) oscillations appear to reflect local processing related to activation and maintenance of neuronal object representations (Jensen et al., 2007), binding diverse perceptual and contextual information (Nyhus and Curran, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gamma oscillations bind diverse perceptual and contextual information.
source: Neocortical and hippocampal gamma (>30 Hz) oscillations appear to reflect local processing related to activation and maintenance of neuronal object representations (Jensen et al., 2007), binding diverse perceptual and contextual information (Nyhus and Curran, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spatially separate gamma oscillations have been found to be locked to the phase of the theta oscillation, supporting binding of the coherent ensemble underlying a given memory trace.
source: Spatially separate gamma oscillations have been found to be locked to the phase of the theta oscillation, supporting binding of the coherent ensemble underlying a given memory trace (Mizuhara and Yamaguchi, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Gamma-power-to-theta-phase cross-frequency coupling (CFC) has been identified within human neocortex during word recognition.
source: Indeed such gamma-power-to-theta-phase cross-frequency coupling (CFC) has been identified within human neocortex during word recognition (Canolty et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Gamma-power-to-theta-phase cross-frequency coupling has been identified during working memory maintenance.
source: working memory maintenance (Axmacher et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Gamma-power-to-theta-phase cross-frequency coupling has been identified in successful long-term memory encoding.
source: and in successful long-term memory encoding (Friese et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Gamma-power-to-theta-phase cross-frequency coupling has been identified within the rat hippocampus.
source: as well as within the rat hippocampus (Colgin et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cross-frequency coupling has been proposed as a mechanism for transiently coupling distributed cortical activity.
source: and has been proposed as a mechanism for transiently coupling distributed cortical activity (Canolty et al., 2006; Friese et al., 2012; Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neocortical-ATN communication might be related to local ATN processing during encoding.
source: Together, these findings suggest that neocortical-ATN communication might be related to local ATN processing during encoding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from prior findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: Neocortical-ATN theta phase synchrony would be critical for memory encoding.
source: We hypothesized that neocortical-ATN theta phase synchrony, and the relationship between theta phase and local ATN gamma amplitudes, would be critical for memory encoding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: The relationship between theta phase and local ATN gamma amplitudes would be critical for memory encoding.
source: We hypothesized that neocortical-ATN theta phase synchrony, and the relationship between theta phase and local ATN gamma amplitudes, would be critical for memory encoding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: All eight participants were able to discriminate old from new scenes.
source: All eight participants were able to discriminate old from new scenes (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data presented in Table 1.

claim: Mean successful encoding across participants was 55%.
source: Mean successful encoding across participants was 55%, and mean unsuccessful encoding was 45%, resulting in means of 101 and 87 observations per category, respectively, for EEG analysis.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral data.

claim: Mean unsuccessful encoding across participants was 45%.
source: Mean successful encoding across participants was 55%, and mean unsuccessful encoding was 45%, resulting in means of 101 and 87 observations per category, respectively, for EEG analysis.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral data.

claim: Response times for the indoor/outdoor judgment at encoding did not differ significantly between successfully and unsuccessfully encoded scenes.
source: Response times for the indoor/outdoor judgment at encoding were compared between successfully (group mean = 1.04 s) and unsuccessfully (group mean = 1.14 s) encoded scenes for the seven participants for whom the paradigm was identical (see 'Materials and methods'), and no difference was detected (paired T-test: T = 1.81, p = 0.12, with 6° of freedom, DF).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The mean difference between expected and observed probabilities of sequential successful encoding across the group did not significantly differ from zero.
source: For each participant, the difference between their expected probability of sequential successful encoding, calculated according to their overall rate of successful encoding, and their observed probability of sequential successful encoding, was calculated. The mean difference between these probabilities across the group did not significantly differ from zero (one-sample T-test: T = 1.35, p = 0.22, with 7 DF).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The behavioral findings suggest that the neural findings did not reflect simple global attentional fluctuations.
source: Both these behavioral findings suggest that the neural findings to be reported did not reflect simple global attentional fluctuations (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Frontal-right-ATN (RATN) theta synchrony was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding at 5–6 Hz between 0.5 and 1.5 s after picture presentation.
source: Frontal-right-ATN (RATN) theta synchrony was indeed greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding at 5–6 Hz between 0.5 and 1.5 s after picture presentation (permutation tests, PT: p = 0.001; paired T-tests, TT: T = 9.9, p = 0.000022; Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in figures.

claim: Conservative false discovery rate correction yielded a threshold of p = 0.0019 for overall criterion p = 0.05.
source: Conservative false discovery rate correction (PT; 57 frequencies, 0–100 Hz; 1024 data-points, 0–2 s) yielded a threshold of p = 0.0019 (overall criterion p = 0.05).
evidence: This describes the statistical correction method applied.

claim: Cluster-size permutation test showed the second cluster of late theta synchrony to be significant.
source: Cluster-size PT (CSPT) on binary TT outcomes (significant/nonsignificant at p = 0.05) showed the second cluster of this late theta synchrony to be significant (∼1.0–1.5 s; p = 0.016; observed contiguous cluster 437 pixels; criterial cluster 285 pixels for overall p = 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Synchrony at 5.2 Hz, averaged from 0.5 to 1.5 s, was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding in seven of eight participants.
source: Synchrony at 5.2 Hz, averaged from 0.5 to 1.5 s for each participant, was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding in seven of eight participants (Figure 2E), yielding a group difference in median synchrony (Wilcoxon test: p = 0.038).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All eight participants showed greater theta synchrony during successful than unsuccessful encoding from 1.25–1.5 s post-stimulus.
source: Note from Figure 2F and Figure 2—supplement 2 that theta synchrony was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding in all eight participants from 1.25–1.5 s post-stimulus
evidence: This is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The appearance of two separate episodes of theta synchrony at the group level is likely due to inter-participant differences in the timing of the synchrony episode over the 1 s time window from 0.5–1.5 s post-stimulus.
source: and the appearance of two separate episodes at the group level is likely to have arisen due to inter-participant differences in the timing of the synchrony episode over the 1 s time window from 0.5–1.5 s post-stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data patterns observed.

claim: The mean PLVs showed a significant interaction between frequency and encoding success when comparing theta (5.2 Hz) and beta (17.5 Hz) wavelets.
source: To further test frequency-specificity, a two-way repeated measures analysis of variance was applied to frontal-RATN PLVs obtained using theta (5.2 Hz) and beta (17.5 Hz) wavelets averaged from 0.5 to 1.5 s for each participant during successful and unsuccessful encoding. The mean PLVs showed a significant interaction between frequency and encoding success (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The interaction between frequency and encoding success remained significant when taking adjacent theta and beta wavelets, and when taking theta and alpha wavelets.
source: This interaction remained significant when taking adjacent theta (4.9 Hz and 5.5 Hz) and beta (16.5 Hz and 18.6 Hz) wavelets, and taking theta (5.2 Hz) and alpha (11.7 Hz) wavelets (all ps < 0.002).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: In all cases the advantage for successful over unsuccessful encoding for theta was greater than for alpha or beta, which showed negligible differences.
source: In all cases the advantage for successful over unsuccessful encoding for theta was greater than for alpha or beta, which showed negligible differences.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The interaction was not significant when taking two theta wavelets.
source: The interaction was not significant when taking two theta wavelets (4.9 Hz and 5.2 Hz: p > 0.30; 5.2 Hz and 5.5 Hz: p > 0.60).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: No significant difference was observed between delta (2–4 Hz) phase synchrony during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding.
source: No significant difference was observed between delta (2–4 Hz) phase synchrony during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the data analysis.

claim: No corresponding significant synchrony differences were observed for DMTN or left ATN.
source: We did not observe corresponding significant synchrony differences for DMTN or left ATN (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the data analysis, shown in a figure.

claim: The difference in theta (5.2 Hz) PLVs between successful and unsuccessful encoding in the RATN 0.5–1.5 s post-stimulus was greater than the difference in the right DMTN.
source: Indeed, on direct comparison, the difference in theta (5.2 Hz) PLVs between successful and unsuccessful encoding in the RATN 0.5–1.5 s post-stimulus was greater than the difference in the right DMTN (Wilcoxon test: p = 0.018), supporting nucleus specificity.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of the data.

claim: A direct comparison of the relevant difference in theta PLVs between RATN and LATN only approached significance.
source: A direct comparison of the relevant difference in theta PLVs between RATN and LATN only approached significance (Wilcoxon test: p = 0.130).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of the data.

claim: The finding that the synchrony difference in RATN was significant, whereas that in LATN was not, accords well with the non-verbal scene stimuli used.
source: While we do not wish to make strong claims about laterality, the finding that the synchrony difference in RATN was significant, whereas that in LATN was not (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), accords well with the non-verbal scene stimuli used (Maillard et al., 2011) (see also 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data pattern and supported by a citation.

claim: There was additional early upper theta and alpha synchrony during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding (∼8–12 Hz; 0–0.2 s).
source: There was additional early upper theta and alpha synchrony during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding (∼8–12 Hz; 0–0.2 s; PT: p = 0.002; TT: T = 5.6, p = 0.00085; CSPT: p = 0.029; observed contiguous cluster 342 pixels; Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in figures.

claim: The early upper theta and alpha synchrony might reflect enhanced item-specific attention and perception during successful encoding.
source: which might reflect enhanced item-specific attention and perception during successful encoding (Düzel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding, supported by a citation.

claim: All synchrony patterns were post-stimulus.
source: All synchrony patterns were post-stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: There was a significantly greater synchrony difference between successful and unsuccessful encoding in upper theta/alpha post-stimulus (0–0.2 s) than in the same frequency range during the 1 s pre-stimulus period.
source: There was a significantly greater synchrony difference between successful and unsuccessful encoding in upper theta/alpha post-stimulus (0–0.2 s) than in the same frequency range during the 1 s pre-stimulus period (Wilcoxon test: p = 0.039).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The difference between pre-stimulus theta synchrony preceding successful compared with unsuccessful encoding was not significant.
source: Furthermore, the difference between pre-stimulus theta synchrony preceding successful compared with unsuccessful encoding was not significant (Wilcoxon test: p = 0.46)
evidence: This is a negative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Post-stimulus, the synchrony difference between successful and unsuccessful encoding was significant.
source: whereas post-stimulus, the synchrony difference between successful and unsuccessful encoding was significant (Wilcoxon test: p = 0.039).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Parietal-RATN and frontal-RATN theta synchrony 0.5–1.5 s post-stimulus were significantly enhanced individually during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding in two participants with parietal electrodes.
source: Because parietal scalp signals could be recorded from only two participants due to post-operative dressing placement, these were also analyzed as individual cases (Figure 2—figure supplements 6–7). Parietal-RATN and frontal-RATN (consistent with the group data) theta synchrony 0.5–1.5 s post-stimulus were significantly enhanced individually during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding (permutation tests on individual epochs within participants: ps < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of individual participant data and shown in figures.

claim: CFC was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding between frontal theta phase-troughs and RATN gamma (∼40–50 Hz) amplitude-peaks.
source: Because the main synchrony findings occurred in theta between 0.5 and 1.5 s, further analyses focussed on this time-frequency range. CFC was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding between frontal theta phase-troughs and RATN gamma (∼40–50 Hz) amplitude-peaks (TT, T = 4.9, p = 0.0018; CSPT: p = 0.038; observed contiguous cluster 14 pixels; criterial cluster 12 pixels for overall p = 0.05; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The CFC difference was absent for thalamic high gamma (up to 256 Hz).
source: The difference was absent for thalamic high gamma (up to 256 Hz) (Canolty et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Within the RATN, theta phase-peaks were coupled with gamma amplitude-peaks.
source: In contrast to the frontal-RATN findings, within the RATN, theta phase-peaks were coupled with gamma amplitude-peaks.
evidence: This is a finding from the CFC analysis.

claim: The gamma range was narrower (∼40–50 Hz compared with ∼40–70 Hz) during successful than during unsuccessful encoding.
source: Of note is that the gamma range was narrower (∼40–50 Hz compared with ∼40–70 Hz) during successful than during unsuccessful encoding
evidence: This is a finding from the CFC analysis.

claim: There was significantly greater within-RATN CFC involving higher gamma-frequency amplitudes during unsuccessful compared with during successful encoding.
source: resulting in significantly greater within-RATN CFC involving higher gamma-frequency amplitudes during unsuccessful compared with during successful encoding (paired T-test, TT, T = 3.6, p = 0.0086; cluster-size permutation test, CSPT: p = 0.045; observed contiguous cluster 15 pixels; criterial cluster 14 pixels for overall p = 0.05; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in a figure supplement.

claim: Within-RATN CFC patterns during successful and unsuccessful encoding differed significantly.
source: The CFC patterns during successful and unsuccessful encoding were then compared directly. Within-RATN CFC during successful encoding was compared with a distribution of 1000 phase-scattered surrogates, and the theta-gamma (3.8–8.1 Hz, 30.5–64.6 Hz) cross-frequency points at which CFC during successful encoding exceeded a threshold with criterion p = 0.05 were identified. The same analysis was performed for unsuccessful encoding. The two resulting CFC patterns differed significantly (two-dimensional Kolmogorov–Smirnov test—2-D KS test: d = 0.81, p = 0.048), with a wider gamma range during unsuccessful encoding.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of CFC patterns.

claim: The narrower RATN gamma range coupled with theta phase during successful memory formation could be interpreted as reflecting firing of only relevant neural assemblies, thus reflecting neural specificity during encoding.
source: Assuming that an assembly of synchronously firing neurons is associated with a particular memory trace, the narrower RATN gamma range coupled with theta phase during successful memory formation could be interpreted as reflecting firing of only relevant neural assemblies, thus reflecting neural specificity during encoding (Desimone, 1996; Düzel et al., 2005; Schott et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding, supported by citations.

claim: The corticothalamic coupling may coordinate the firing of particular thalamic neural assemblies underpinning the memory to be encoded, facilitating synaptic strengthening and relevant memory formation.
source: We correspondingly postulate that the corticothalamic coupling may coordinate the firing of particular thalamic neural assemblies underpinning the memory to be encoded, facilitating synaptic strengthening and relevant memory formation.
evidence: This is a postulation based on the findings.

claim: Ongoing CFC has been detected in the centromedian thalamic nucleus during cognitive task performance.
source: Indeed, ongoing CFC has been detected in the centromedian thalamic nucleus during cognitive task performance (Fitzgerald et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There was no encoding-related CFC difference apparent for thalamic high gamma.
source: Again, there was no encoding-related CFC difference apparent for thalamic high gamma (Canolty et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Theta-to-gamma CFC was peak-to-peak at higher theta frequencies within the frontal cortex, and occurred for both successful and unsuccessful encoding.
source: CFC findings within the frontal cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F) were consistent with the literature. Theta-to-gamma CFC was peak-to-peak at higher theta frequencies, and occurred for both successful and unsuccessful encoding (phase-scattered surrogate-data tests for successful and for unsuccessful encoding: p = 0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the CFC analysis, shown in a figure supplement.

claim: There was no significant relationship between frontal peak-to-peak theta-to-gamma CFC and encoding success.
source: There was no significant relationship to encoding success (TT, p > 0.05; CSPT: p > 0.05; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F), consistent with hippocampal CFC patterns during working memory (Axmacher et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the data analysis, consistent with prior research.

claim: Theta-to-gamma CFC was trough-to-peak at lower theta frequencies within the frontal cortex, and was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding.
source: By contrast, theta-to-gamma CFC was trough-to-peak at lower theta frequencies, and was greater during successful than unsuccessful encoding (TT, T = 3.6, p = 0.0087; CSPT: p = 0.017; observed contiguous cluster 19 pixels; criterial cluster 11 pixels for overall p = 0.05), consistent with (Canolty et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from the CFC analysis, consistent with prior research.

claim: Theta-gamma CFC patterns within RATN and within frontal neocortex differed from the frontal-RATN pattern.
source: Theta-gamma CFC patterns within RATN and within frontal neocortex differed from the frontal-RATN pattern (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of CFC patterns shown in figure supplements.

claim: Frontal-RATN theta-gamma coupling during successful vs unsuccessful encoding differed significantly from within-RATN CFC.
source: Frontal-RATN theta-gamma (3.8–8.1 Hz, 30.5–64.6 Hz) coupling during successful vs unsuccessful encoding was compared using the above paired T-tests, to provide the cross-frequency pattern, and the same was performed for within-RATN CFC. These CFC patterns differed significantly (2-D KS test: d = 0.83, p = 0.024).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of CFC patterns.

claim: Frontal-RATN and within-frontal CFC patterns differed significantly.
source: Frontal-RATN and within-frontal CFC patterns also differed significantly (2-D KS test: d = 0.98, p = 0.011).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of CFC patterns.

claim: Granger causality revealed that frontal theta better predicted RATN theta than vice-versa.
source: GC revealed that frontal theta better predicted RATN theta than vice-versa (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from Granger causality analysis, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Frontal theta prediction of RATN theta peaked at a model-order of 32, which corresponds to 63 ms, or one third of a theta cycle phase-lag between frontal and RATN theta.
source: In GC analyses, the peak model order provides an indication of how far into the past one signal provides information about another, and may thus be interpreted as indicating the approximate delay in transfer of information (Staudigl et al., 2012). We found that frontal theta prediction of RATN theta peaked at a model-order of 32, which corresponds to 63 ms, or one third of a theta cycle phase-lag between frontal and RATN theta.
evidence: This is a finding from Granger causality analysis.

claim: The delay of 63 ms is broadly consistent with frontal-RATN theta-to-gamma CFC being trough-to-peak, and intra-RATN theta-to-gamma CFC being peak-to-peak.
source: Such a delay is broadly consistent with frontal-RATN theta-to-gamma CFC being trough-to-peak (Figure 3), and intra-RATN theta-to-gamma CFC being peak-to-peak (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Granger causality and CFC findings.

claim: The CFC and GC findings suggest that frontal theta modulates RATN gamma via frontal-ATN theta synchrony during successful encoding.
source: Together, the CFC and GC findings suggest that frontal theta modulates RATN gamma via frontal-ATN theta synchrony during successful encoding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined CFC and Granger causality findings.

claim: The study demonstrates increased corticothalamic synchrony during successful memory encoding.
source: We demonstrate increased corticothalamic synchrony during successful memory encoding, recording directly from the two most memory-relevant thalamic nuclei (ATN and DMTN).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Timing of post-stimulus ATN theta activity alone, and its relation to local ATN processing as indexed by gamma amplitudes, is critical in successful memory encoding.
source: Our amplitude-independent phase synchrony measurements (Lachaux et al., 1999) show that timing of post-stimulus ATN theta activity alone (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 8), and its relation to local ATN processing as indexed by gamma amplitudes, is critical in successful memory encoding
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phase synchrony and CFC findings.

claim: The findings provide the first electrophysiological evidence concerning the role of ATN in human memory formation.
source: providing the first electrophysiological evidence concerning the role of ATN in human memory formation.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: The absence of neocortical-DMTN synchrony differences, together with their recent detection during verbal memory retrieval, fits with evidence suggesting ATN specialization for encoding and DMTN for retrieval.
source: The absence of neocortical-DMTN synchrony differences, together with their recent detection during verbal memory retrieval (Staudigl et al., 2012), fits with evidence suggesting ATN specialization for encoding (Harding et al., 2000; Van der Werf et al., 2003), and DMTN for retrieval (Harding et al., 2000; Van der Werf et al., 2003; Aggleton et al., 2010; Aggleton, 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior research.

claim: RATN involvement is consistent with the non-verbal scene stimuli employed.
source: RATN involvement is moreover consistent with the non-verbal scene stimuli employed (Maillard et al., 2011)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: RATN involvement is consistent with evidence that left thalamus lesions produce more severe memory deficits for verbal than non-verbal material.
source: and with evidence that left thalamus lesions produce more severe memory deficits for verbal than non-verbal material (Squire et al., 1989).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: The late theta synchrony is in accord with the timing of differences in ERPs and post-stimulus MT theta power during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding of episodic memories.
source: The late theta synchrony is in accord with the timing of differences in ERPs (Schott et al., 2002) and post-stimulus MT theta power (Hanslmayr and Staudigl, 2014) during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding of episodic memories.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior research.

claim: Oscillations in the delta frequency range have recently been found to show a memory-related difference in the hippocampus.
source: While oscillations in the delta frequency range have recently been found to show a memory-related difference in the hippocampus (Watrous et al., 2011; Lega et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Item-specific attention has a well-recognized effect on whether an item is successfully encoded.
source: Item-specific attention indeed has a well-recognized effect on whether an item is successfully encoded (Raz and Buhle, 2006; Muzzio et al., 2009; Kim, 2011; Burke et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attention is not only necessary for optimal memory encoding, but multiple brain structures involved in memory formation may be subject to attentional modulation, including the hippocampus itself.
source: Attention is not only necessary for optimal memory encoding, but multiple brain structures involved in memory formation may be subject to attentional modulation, including the hippocampus itself (Muzzio et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The timing of the key memory differences at around 1 s post-stimulus is strongly suggestive of a memory-related difference.
source: Firstly, the timing of the key memory differences here at around 1 s post-stimulus is strongly suggestive of a memory-related difference.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing of the findings.

claim: Neural encoding differences related to later memory have been identified using ERPs and cortical theta/gamma oscillations, generally peaking at around 1 s after stimulus presentation, continuing up to 1.5 s post-stimulus.
source: Neural encoding differences related to later memory have been identified using ERPs and cortical theta/gamma oscillations, generally peaking at around 1 s after stimulus presentation, continuing up to 1.5 s post-stimulus (Paller et al., 1987; Schott et al., 2002; Sederberg et al., 2003; Osipova et al., 2006; Lega et al., 2012; Hanslmayr and Staudigl, 2014; Long et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Oscillatory dynamics between the pulvinar thalamic nucleus and the parietal cortex support visual attention in macaques, consistent with attention deficits following focal pulvinar lesions.
source: Secondly, whereas oscillatory dynamics between the pulvinar thalamic nucleus and the parietal cortex support visual attention in macaques, consistent with attention deficits following focal pulvinar lesions (Saalmann et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Based on current knowledge about the ATN and the DMTN, one would expect attentional differences to be reflected in DMTN activity.
source: Moreover, based on current knowledge about the ATN and the DMTN (Van der Werf et al., 2003) one would rather expect attentional differences to be reflected in DMTN activity, which we did not find.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior knowledge and the current findings.

claim: If global attentional fluctuations were responsible for the theta synchrony findings, one would expect longer response times during the encoding phase for later forgotten compared with later remembered scenes.
source: Most critically, if global attentional fluctuations were responsible for our theta synchrony findings, one would expect longer response times during the encoding phase for later forgotten compared with later remembered scenes, due to lack of attention to the encoding task. However, response times did not differ.
evidence: This is a logical inference used to argue against an alternative explanation.

claim: Global attentional fluctuations over time would imply a dependency between the probability of successful encoding on successive trials during the study phase of the experiment.
source: Finally, global attentional fluctuations over time would also imply a dependency between the probability of successful encoding on successive trials during the study phase of the experiment, and we found no dependency.
evidence: This is a logical inference used to argue against an alternative explanation, supported by the behavioral data.

claim: Variability in factors such as attention and the emotional valence of stimuli are fundamental to the study design in subsequent memory paradigms.
source: We note, however, that variability in factors such as attention and the emotional valence of stimuli are fundamental to the study design in subsequent memory paradigms, affecting the probability of successfully encoding each item and thus enabling comparison of successful with unsuccessful encoding.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of subsequent memory paradigms.

claim: The ATN is the target of stimulation in the treatment of focal epilepsy on the basis that seizure activity starting focally is propagated through this site to widespread cortical areas.
source: The ATN is the target of stimulation in the treatment of focal epilepsy on the basis that seizure activity starting focally is propagated through this site to widespread cortical areas (Lega et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Regional cortical specificity in frontal-RATN synchrony would support the argument that the differences identified are memory-specific.
source: Regional cortical specificity in frontal-RATN synchrony would support our argument that the differences that we have identified are memory-specific.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would strengthen the interpretation of the findings.

claim: The phase synchrony pattern is discernible in all three electrode placements (frontopolar, other frontal, and parietal), but is not identical across regions.
source: While the phase synchrony pattern we report is discernible in all three electrode placements (frontopolar, other frontal, and parietal), it is indeed not identical across regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in a figure supplement.

claim: Both frontal and parietal cortices are well-recognized as being involved in memory processing.
source: We note also, though, that both frontal and parietal cortices are well-recognized as being involved in memory processing (Weiss and Rappelsberger, 2000; Otten et al., 2002; Sauseng et al., 2005; Uncapher and Wagner, 2009; Friese et al., 2012; Sweeney-Reed et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The encoding and retrieval tasks were chosen for their simplicity, because recording was only possible at the bedside in the few days following intracranial surgery.
source: The encoding and retrieval tasks were chosen for their simplicity, because recording was only possible at the bedside in the few days following intracranial surgery, and because we did not wish to lose data owing to failure of these rare participants to succeed at the tasks.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: A limitation of the study is that the results cannot be conclusively linked to recollection, and therefore episodic memory formation, separately from familiarity.
source: Thus, a limitation of the study is that we cannot conclusively link our results to recollection, and therefore episodic memory formation, separately from familiarity.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: The findings concerning ATN electrophysiological involvement in human memory formation are consistent with the theoretical proposal that the ATN is a part of an extended hippocampal system supporting episodic recollection.
source: Our findings concerning ATN electrophysiological involvement in human memory formation are, however, consistent with the theoretical proposal that the ATN is a part of an extended hippocampal system supporting episodic recollection (Aggleton, 2012), whether during encoding or retrieval
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior theory.

claim: The findings are consistent with the competing theoretical proposal that the ATN is specialized for encoding rather than retrieval, whether the information involved is episodic (recollection) or semantic.
source: and with the competing theoretical proposal that the ATN is specialized for encoding rather than retrieval, whether the information involved is episodic (recollection) or semantic (Van der Werf et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior theory.

claim: The latter proposal is consistent with human lesion data, showing that sufferers from Korsakoff's syndrome with lesions to the ATN fail to acquire new semantic as well as new episodic information.
source: The latter proposal is consistent with human lesion data, showing that sufferers from Korsakoff's syndrome with lesions to the ATN fail to acquire new semantic as well as new episodic information (for example, Harding et al., 2000) and is thus particularly consistent with our new data.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Whether recollection and familiarity are separate processes, or reflect a single process with different degrees of memory strength, is an area of continuing debate.
source: We note, furthermore, that whether recollection and familiarity are separate processes (Eichenbaum et al., 2008), or reflect a single process, with familiarity and recollection reflecting different degrees of memory strength (Wixted and Squire, 2008), is an area of continuing debate (see also Gardiner and Richardson-Klavehn, 2000 and Yonelinas, 2002) for relevant information regarding humans.
evidence: This is a statement about an ongoing debate in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Despite the lack of behavioral/psychological resolution, the data provide novel evidence concerning the real-time role of the human ATN in memory formation.
source: Despite this lack of behavioral/psychological resolution, our data nevertheless provide novel evidence concerning the real-time role of the human ATN in memory formation.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the findings despite acknowledged limitations.

claim: Memory processing may be divided into different subsystems, with different components of memory processing involving different thalamic nuclei.
source: It should also be noted that memory processing may be divided into different subsystems, with different components of memory processing involving different thalamic nuclei (Mennemeier et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The nucleus reuniens is involved in fear conditioning and memory generalization.
source: For example, evidence supports a role for the nucleus reuniens in fear conditioning and memory generalization (Vertes et al., 2007; Xu and Südhof, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The nucleus reuniens is involved in spatial processing.
source: as well as spatial processing (Jankowski et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The pulvinar nucleus is involved in attention and nonverbal memory processing.
source: for the pulvinar nucleus in attention (Saalmann et al., 2012) and nonverbal memory processing (Johnson and Ojemann, 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The left ventro-lateral thalamus is involved in verbal memory encoding.
source: and for the left ventro-lateral thalamus in verbal memory encoding (Johnson and Ojemann, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The focus on the ATN and DMTN is based on the rare availability of human electrophysiological data from these sites, which was determined by clinical requirements.
source: Our focus on the ATN and DMTN is based on the rare availability of human electrophysiological data from these sites, which was determined by clinical requirements, and is consistent with extant data concerning the amnesic effects of lesions in these thalamic areas in humans (Harding et al., 2000; Van der Werf et al., 2003).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the focus of the study.

claim: The findings shed new light on real-time interaction between the ATN and the neocortex, broadening understanding of the brain structures involved in memory formation from a focus on the hippocampus and neocortex to recognition of a pivotal role for the ATN.
source: In summary, our findings shed new light on real-time interaction between the ATN and the neocortex, thus broadening understanding of the brain structures involved in memory formation from a focus on the hippocampus and neocortex to recognition of a pivotal role for the ATN.
evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the findings.

claim: The CFC theta-gamma findings, together with the amnesic effects of lesions to the human ATN, provide evidence that the ATN plays an active role in encoding, instead of simply relaying cortical or hippocampal signals.
source: More generally, the CFC theta-gamma findings, together with the amnesic effects of lesions to the human ATN, provide evidence that the ATN plays an active role in encoding, instead of simply relaying cortical or hippocampal signals (Aggleton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings and prior lesion data.

claim: Intrathalamic data were recorded from 1.5 mm platinum-iridium electrodes implanted bilaterally (four contacts each) in the thalamus for stimulation therapy for multiple pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy in eight adult participants.
source: Intrathalamic data were recorded from 1.5 mm platinum-iridium electrodes implanted bilaterally (four contacts each) in the thalamus for stimulation therapy for multiple pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy in eight adult participants, all of whom were not suitable candidates for resective surgery.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and participant characteristics.

claim: Memory-dependent phase synchrony has been detected on an individual level in intracranial recordings.
source: A minimum sample size was not set, because memory-dependent phase synchrony has been detected on an individual level in intracranial recordings (Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Staudigl et al., 2012) (see also Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 6–7).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mean age of the participants was 37.5 years (range 28–52 years, standard deviation 8.2 years), and four participants were female.
source: The mean age of the participants was 37.5 years (range 28–52 years, standard deviation 8.2 years), and four participants were female.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics.

claim: Stimulation via intracranial electrodes did not occur during the data recording.
source: Stimulation via intracranial electrodes did not occur during the data recording.
evidence: This describes an aspect of the experimental procedure.

claim: Contacts were located in the ATN for all eight participants and in the DMTN for seven of the participants.
source: Contacts were located in the ATN for all eight participants and in the DMTN for seven of the participants (with Participant 5 not having DMTN contacts).
evidence: This describes the electrode locations.

claim: Placement of the thalamic electrodes was performed stereotactically.
source: Placement of the thalamic electrodes was performed stereotactically.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.

claim: An intra-operative X-ray and postoperative CT-scans were carried out in order to confirm correct localization of each electrode.
source: An intra-operative X-ray and postoperative CT-scans were carried out in order to confirm correct localization of each electrode, by reference to the Schaltenbrand and Pick Atlases (Schaltenbrand and Wahren, 1977; Maldjian et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the verification procedure for electrode placement.

claim: Scalp EEG data were simultaneously collected from frontal electrodes (Fz, AFz, or Fpz) in all eight participants.
source: Scalp EEG data were simultaneously collected from frontal electrodes (Fz, AFz, or Fpz) in all eight participants
evidence: This describes the data collection procedure.

claim: Scalp EEG data were collected from parietal electrodes only in Participant 1 (P3, Pz, P4) and Participant 2 (Pz only).
source: and from parietal electrodes only in Participant 1 (P3, Pz, P4; Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 6) and Participant 2 (Pz only; Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This describes the data collection procedure.

claim: Positioning of post-operative dressings meant that parietal electrodes could not be placed for six participants.
source: Positioning of post-operative dressings meant that parietal electrodes could not be placed for the other six participants.
evidence: This explains a limitation in the data collection.

claim: Frontal electrodes were centered over Fz (frontal), AFz (anterior frontal), and Fpz (frontopolar), with the data from the most frontal available electrode from each participant included in the group analyses.
source: Frontal electrodes were centered over Fz (frontal), AFz (anterior frontal), and Fpz (frontopolar), with the data from the most frontal available electrode from each participant included in the group analyses.
evidence: This describes the electrode placement and data selection.

claim: These scalp sites reflect underlying cortical activity from midline frontal cortices.
source: These scalp sites reflect underlying cortical activity from midline frontal cortices (Paller et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Nose-referenced voltages were amplified with a Walter Graphtek (Lübeck, Germany) EEG amplifier and recorded with a 512 Hz sampling frequency.
source: Nose-referenced voltages were amplified with a Walter Graphtek (Lübeck, Germany) EEG amplifier and recorded with a 512 Hz sampling frequency.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition equipment and parameters.

claim: Offline re-referencing of thalamic voltages to the next deepest contact rendered six bipolar channels.
source: Offline re-referencing of thalamic voltages to the next deepest contact rendered six bipolar channels.
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure.

claim: No measureable temporal phase-shifts that simply reflect the physical properties of the brain-to-scalp-electrode interface have been detected at typical EEG frequencies.
source: Note that no measureable temporal phase-shifts that simply reflect the physical (e.g., capacitative) properties of the brain-to-scalp-electrode interface have been detected at typical EEG frequencies (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Any phase-lags between the scalp and intrathalamic recordings should reflect genuine neural conduction delays between neocortex and thalamus.
source: Any phase-lags between the scalp and intrathalamic recordings should, therefore, reflect genuine neural conduction delays between neocortex and thalamus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of physical phase-shifts.

claim: Phase-lags should not affect the corticothalamic phase synchrony measurements, which were independent of phase-lag as well as amplitude.
source: Such phase-lags should not in any case affect the corticothalamic phase synchrony measurements detailed below, which were independent of phase-lag as well as amplitude, but were taken into account in the Granger causality calculations detailed below.
evidence: This describes a property of the analysis method.

claim: During encoding, the participants viewed a series of 200 (100 for Participant 1) photographs of unfamiliar real-world scenes on a computer screen.
source: During encoding, the participants viewed a series of 200 (100 for Participant 1) photographs of unfamiliar real-world scenes on a computer screen.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Each scene was shown for 2.4 s, followed by a fixation cross for 1.4 s.
source: Each scene was shown for 2.4 s, followed by a fixation cross for 1.4 s
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The participant judged whether the depicted scene was indoors or outdoors (average response time around 1 s after scene presentation).
source: and the participant judged whether the depicted scene was indoors or outdoors (average response time around 1 s after scene presentation).
evidence: This describes the experimental task and behavioral data.

claim: Recognition testing occurred after a short distraction break to ensure retrieval based on long-term memory.
source: Recognition testing occurred after a short distraction break to ensure retrieval based on long-term memory.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Each participant viewed all 200 scenes from the encoding phase in a different random order, randomly interspersed with 100 similar but new scenes.
source: Each participant viewed all 200 scenes from the encoding phase in a different random order, randomly interspersed with 100 similar but new scenes.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: A short practice session with both encoding and recognition test phases was provided for each participant, rendering the experiment itself an intentional encoding paradigm.
source: A short practice session with both encoding and recognition test phases was provided for each participant, rendering the experiment itself an intentional encoding paradigm, because participants knew during encoding that they would later be tested.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The focus of the encoding task was on deciding whether each depicted scene was indoors or outdoors.
source: Nevertheless, the focus of the encoding task was on deciding whether each depicted scene was indoors or outdoors.
evidence: This describes the experimental task.

claim: In the recognition test, each scene was first shown for 1.25 s, then a 6-point scale was superimposed on the scene for 2.8 s.
source: In the recognition test, each scene was first shown for 1.25 s, then a 6-point scale was superimposed on the scene for 2.8 s, along which a marker was moved by pressing one of two keyboard buttons, with the index finger of each hand, to indicate degrees of confidence as to whether the scene was old or new (direction and response hand counterbalanced across participants).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The data presented were collapsed across the three scale points indicating 'old', and the three scale points indicating 'new' at test, to obtain binary 'old'/'new' judgments.
source: The data presented here were collapsed across the three scale points indicating 'old', and the three scale points indicating 'new' at test, to obtain binary 'old'/'new' judgments.
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure.

claim: The encoding data were sorted, according to test phase responses, into epochs with successful encoding (later correct 'old' judgments to old scenes at test, hits) and epochs with unsuccessful encoding (later incorrect 'new' judgments to old scenes at test, misses).
source: The encoding data (electrophysiological data and response times) were then sorted, according to test phase responses, into epochs with successful encoding (later correct 'old' judgments to old scenes at test, hits) and epochs with unsuccessful encoding (later incorrect 'new' judgments to old scenes at test, misses) (Paller and Wagner, 2002).
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure.

claim: The electrophysiological encoding data were segmented into epochs 1 s pre-stimulus to 2 s post-stimulus.
source: The electrophysiological encoding data were segmented into epochs 1 s pre-stimulus (i.e., scene presentation at encoding) to 2 s post-stimulus
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure.

claim: Recording of intracranial signals was performed at the bedside in the few days following electrode implantation, before the electrodes were attached to a stimulator under the skin over the chest wall for epilepsy treatment.
source: Recording of intracranial signals was performed at the bedside in the few days following electrode implantation, before the electrodes were attached to a stimulator under the skin over the chest wall for epilepsy treatment, in a second operation approximately 1 week later.
evidence: This describes the timing and context of data collection.

claim: No seizures took place during the testing sessions, and all patients were fully alert and cooperative throughout.
source: No seizures took place during the testing sessions, and all patients were fully alert and cooperative throughout.
evidence: This describes the condition of participants during data collection.

claim: Epochs were individually visually inspected and cleaned of ocular and other artifacts using temporal-decorrelation-separation independent component analysis.
source: Epochs were individually visually inspected and cleaned of ocular and other artifacts using temporal-decorrelation-separation independent component analysis (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure.

claim: Spikes and spike-waves were removed using temporal-decorrelation-separation independent component analysis, to maximize the number of epochs for analysis.
source: Spikes and spike-waves were also removed using this approach, to maximize the number of epochs for analysis.
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure.

claim: The differences in electrophysiological activity detected between epochs recorded during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding are unlikely to result from global attentional fluctuations due to epileptiform activity.
source: We deemed the differences in electrophysiological activity detected between epochs recorded during successful compared with unsuccessful encoding in our simple task to be unlikely to result from global attentional fluctuations due to epileptiform activity for several reasons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Accuracy was close to ceiling for the indoor vs outdoor judgment during encoding.
source: Firstly, accuracy was close to ceiling for the indoor vs outdoor judgment during encoding.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding.

claim: While the cortical site of the epileptic focus differed across participants, the reported results were highly consistent across the group.
source: Furthermore, while the cortical site of the epileptic focus differed across participants (Table 2), the reported results were highly consistent across the group (Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 6–7).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in figures and table.

claim: Spikes or spike-waves were visible in the data from three of the eight participants.
source: Spikes or spike-waves were visible in the data from three of the eight participants (Participant 2: 10.3% during successful and 7.3% during unsuccessful encoding; Participant 6: 29.9% and 24.7% respectively; Participant 7: 2.7% and 5.4% respectively).
evidence: This describes the presence of epileptiform activity in the data.

claim: Across the three participants with spikes or spike-waves, the mean difference in these percentages between successful and unsuccessful encoding was only 1.83%.
source: Across these three participants, the mean difference in these percentages between successful and unsuccessful encoding was only 1.83% (i.e., slightly greater for successful encoding), suggesting that concerns about spikes and spike-waves being confounded with the two data categories of interest are minimal.
evidence: This is a calculation from the data used to argue against a confound.

claim: The analyses were also performed excluding epochs with spikes and spike-waves, and the findings reported remained statistically significant.
source: Nevertheless, the analyses were also performed excluding epochs with spikes and spike-waves, and the findings reported remained statistically significant.
evidence: This describes an additional analysis performed to address a potential confound.
